clue.text: Synod here made very little by following Rome

parts.note: a whit is the smallest amount, as in 'not a whit'
taken as written

explanation.surface: A church council talks itself small by deciding to toe Rome's line.
explanation.walkthrough: The Synod of Whitby (664) settled the English church on Roman rather than Celtic practice, so 'following Rome' is the scene, not wordplay; 'made' links.
explanation.definitionFit: The Yorkshire abbey town hosted the famous seventh-century church council, so it is the synod's location.

clue.text: Departed with value but executed for treason

parts.note: went means departed
worth means value

explanation.surface: Someone who left with their fortune but was beheaded as a traitor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' links. Thomas Wentworth, Earl of Strafford, adviser to Charles I, was executed for treason in 1641.
explanation.definitionFit: The Earl of Strafford, Charles I's minister, was attainted and beheaded on Tower Hill in 1641.

clue.text: The last of Rackstraw's might-have-beens

parts.note: in HMS Pinafore the sailor Ralph Rackstraw might have been a Russian, French, Turk, Prussian, or finally a native of Rome's country

explanation.surface: The final item in a sailor's list of other lives he might have led.
explanation.walkthrough: Gilbert and Sullivan's song 'For he is an Englishman' lists what Ralph Rackstraw 'might have been'; the last nationality named is this.
explanation.definitionFit: The song's list of nationalities ends with someone from the country whose capital is Rome.

clue.text: Bright strapping Captain's convertible

parts.note: brass is bright, shiny metal
bound means tied with straps

explanation.surface: A captain's shiny sports car with its roof strapped down.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaw's play is 'Captain Brassbound's Conversion', so the Captain's convertible is a pun on the title; 'strapping' means tying up, not sturdy.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw's play title names the captain who undergoes a conversion, so the convertible one is this captain.

clue.text: Times reform took in the probable cost

indicators.note: to reform the word is to reshape it, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: ate means consumed or took in food

explanation.surface: A newspaper overhaul swallows the expected bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reform' rearranges TIMES into ESTIM, and ATE follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: A rough calculation of what a job will come to is a quote of its likely price.

clue.text: Birds making piles at bridge

definitions.meaning: speckled songbirds that gather in big flocks
a ring of piles driven round a bridge pier to protect it from the current

explanation.surface: Birds building nests beneath a bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making' links. The second sense is engineering: the protective piling round old bridge piers, as at old London Bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Common speckled songbirds; also the protective timber pilings set round the piers of a bridge.

clue.text: Interested in this nation's manner of speaking

indicators.note: this stands for the answer, which put before the word nation gives a manner of speaking, so take the nation away

parts.note: the rise and fall of the voice in speech
nation is taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone keen on how a country talks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'this' means the answer itself: answer + NATION makes a word for a manner of speaking, so removing NATION leaves it.
explanation.definitionFit: Being keen on something is colloquially being 'big on' it, the informal sense of the four-letter preposition.

clue.text: Laurie groom is heard to make things lively

indicators.note: is heard means the phrase is spoken, giving a word that sounds like it

parts.note: in Little Women Laurie marries Amy March, so he is an Amy mate

explanation.surface: A groom named Laurie seems to bring the party to life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is heard': Laurie becomes Amy March's husband in Little Women, so the groom is 'an Amy mate', said as one word.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring life to something or set it in motion is to enliven it.

clue.text: She is among the well-endowed

indicators.note: is among signals the name sits inside the next words

explanation.surface: A woman counted among the rich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is among' hides the name across WELL-ENDOWED; 'She' is the definition, a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name, and any woman can be called she.

clue.text: Entrenched fence — with split sides?

definitions.meaning: a boundary wall sunk in a ditch so it does not block the view
laughing so hard one's sides split

explanation.surface: A fence in a trench, its sides burst open.
explanation.walkthrough: A ha-ha is a sunken fence in an English landscape garden; it is also the sound of laughter.
explanation.definitionFit: A sunken garden barrier set in a ditch; also the sound of hearty laughter.

clue.text: Turn again Gainsborough, the downpour doesn't hold up

indicators.note: turn tells us to read the word again in the opposite direction

parts.note: the painter Thomas Gainsborough was a founding Royal Academician, RA

explanation.surface: A call to the painter Gainsborough to come back, with the rain refusing to stop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn' turns AGAIN into NIAGA; RA (Royal Academician) follows. The definition is cryptic: the great falls are water that never holds itself up.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous falls on the US-Canada border are a cascade of water that simply plunges down.

clue.text: Tempting eminence to a pangolin

parts.note: a small rise that would lure the scaly anteater, since its heap is full of insects to lick up

explanation.surface: A hill that would draw a scaly anteater.
explanation.definitionFit: Pangolins feed on ants, so a mound built by those insects is a raised spot a pangolin would find inviting.

clue.text: Here in Kent the natives are a close lot

definitions.text: Here in Kent the natives are a close lot

parts.words: Here in Kent the natives are a close lot
parts.note: natives are oysters, and a closed oyster is shut tight, so the town is the Kentish oyster harbour

explanation.surface: A Kentish town whose locals keep themselves to themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'natives' are native oysters; this Kent seaside town is famous for them, and a live oyster keeps its shell close shut.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kent coastal town is famous for its native oysters, shellfish that keep firmly shut.

clue.text: Agricultural coverage of naval graduate

parts.note: BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a graduate
RN is the Royal Navy, so naval

explanation.surface: A farming column written by a former navy man with a degree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' links; the pieces go in answer order, the graduate first.
explanation.definitionFit: A farm building puts a roof over crops and livestock, so it is farming shelter.

clue.text: Cuss Reg, Ron — devious sponging lot

indicators.note: devious means following a winding course, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Curse Reg and Ron, a crooked bunch of freeloaders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'devious' rearranges CUSS, REG and RON.
explanation.definitionFit: Cadgers who live off others are freeloaders, a sponging bunch.

clue.text: Terminate telephone or other engagement

parts.note: to end a phone call is to hang up; an engagement is also ended when the betrothal band is removed

explanation.surface: Instructions to end a call or cancel some other appointment.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense: a broken engagement means the ring is taken off.
explanation.definitionFit: Hanging up a phone call is the old phrase here, and a removed betrothal band also ends a marriage engagement.

clue.text: But coming from a kidnapper it calls for payment

definitions.text: But coming from a kidnapper it calls for payment

parts.words: But coming from a kidnapper it calls for payment
parts.note: a sales phrase meaning no charge, read as a kidnapper's ransom terms for releasing a captive

explanation.surface: A warning that a kidnapper's generous-sounding deal costs money.
explanation.walkthrough: A shop's no-cost promotion becomes, from a kidnapper, an offer to set the victim free on payment.
explanation.definitionFit: A promotion that costs nothing; a kidnapper would offer to release someone for ransom.

clue.text: You, Uncle Sam, possible centre of the atomic age

indicators.note: possible signals one possible arrangement of the letters given

parts.note: U is the textspeak spelling of you
Sam is shortened to its initial

explanation.surface: Uncle Sam addressed as a likely hub of the nuclear era.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possible' rearranges U, UNCLE and S. The definition plays on the atom's core in the age of atomic power.
explanation.definitionFit: The core of an atom is its central part, made of protons and neutrons.

clue.text: Bicipital tactics against trouble

parts.note: methods of the biceps, i.e. force and muscle, used against opposition

explanation.surface: Muscle-bound methods for dealing with problems.
explanation.walkthrough: Bicipital means of the biceps, the upper-arm muscle; the phrase describes using force or intimidation.
explanation.definitionFit: Coercive methods rely on physical force, like a powerful upper-arm muscle.

clue.text: Hacks come cheaper than these for some

definitions.text: Hacks come cheaper than these for some

parts.words: Hacks come cheaper than these for some
parts.note: a jibe that some hired writers are worth less than coins worth half a penny

explanation.surface: A sneer that some journalists cost less than small change.
explanation.walkthrough: Ha'pence were old British halfpenny coins, the smallest everyday money; the clue mocks cheap hack writers.
explanation.definitionFit: Halfpennies were tiny British coins, so being cheaper than them means being almost worthless.

clue.text: Nibble for Pater Tendertoe

parts.note: pater is father, pop
a corn is a sore patch on a toe

explanation.surface: A snack for a father with sore feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' links. Pater is old public-school slang for father.
explanation.definitionFit: Puffed maize kernels are a snack to munch.

clue.text: Mohock with scrubbing brush

definitions.meaning: Mohocks were aristocratic thugs roaming London streets at night in the early 1700s
a pad or brush for scraping pans clean

explanation.surface: A street ruffian arrives armed with a brush for the floors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' links the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Eighteenth-century London night-gangs who beat passers-by were known by this name; it is also a cleaning pad for rubbing pots.

clue.text: The others I have are refractory

parts.note: the rest means the others
I've is a contraction of I have

explanation.surface: Someone complaining that everyone else they know is stubborn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'are' links; the definition is an adjective, unruly.
explanation.definitionFit: Restless and unruly, refusing to be controlled, is the sense of stubborn resistance.

clue.text: Where a record's made by climbers

definitions.text: Where a record's made by climbers

parts.note: LP is a long-playing record, with the S of the possessive kept

explanation.surface: Where mountaineers set records.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines: the great European range is where climbers set records, and A plus LP'S spells it.
explanation.definitionFit: The great European mountain range is the classic arena for mountaineering feats.

clue.text: Poet Russell's work? He was fabulous

parts.note: the Irish poet George Russell wrote under the pen-name AE
op, opus, is a work

explanation.surface: A question about a poem by Russell, followed by praise of him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fabulous' means telling fables: the Greek storyteller wrote them.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Greek storyteller is famous for fables, so he was literally fable-telling.

clue.text: Ply oars and step ashore lad; what a picture you could make!

definitions.text: what a picture you could make!

parts.note: to ply oars is to row
to land is to come ashore
a son is a lad

explanation.surface: Someone telling a boy to row in and come ashore, admiring the scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' links. Thomas Rowlandson was a Georgian caricaturist, so the boy rowing ashore could 'make a picture' of his own name.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Rowlandson was an English artist famous for comic drawings of Georgian life.

clue.text: Right of having been among the Psalmist's pots?

definitions.meaning: a legal right to hold property until a debt is paid

definitions.text: having been among the Psalmist's pots?
definitions.meaning: Psalm 68 in the King James Bible says 'though ye have ... among the pots', an old past participle of lie

explanation.surface: A question about a right acquired by lying among old cooking pots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' links. The second sense is archaic: the old past participle of lie, meaning lain.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal claim over goods as security for a debt; also an old form meaning lain.

clue.text: Benefit of footwear

definitions.meaning: a sturdy shoe covering the ankle

explanation.surface: An advantage of good shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' links; 'to boot' preserves the old sense of advantage or profit.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic word for profit or advantage; also a sturdy shoe.

clue.text: Ostentatious fellow at close of play

definitions.meaning: someone who flaunts himself to impress
when the performance ends, the show is over

explanation.surface: A braggart turns up as the game or performance ends.
explanation.definitionFit: A braggart who flaunts himself; also, when a performance ends, the show is called off.

clue.text: Fruit-stealer with blue back in novel guise

parts.note: Eve took the forbidden fruit in Eden

indicators.note: back says the word for blue is read from end to start

parts.note: anil is indigo, a blue dye

explanation.surface: Eve, dressed in blue, turns up in a new disguise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns ANIL to LINA after EVE. 'with' links; 'novel' means a book, not new.
explanation.definitionFit: Fanny Burney's 1778 book takes its title from its heroine, so she appears as a novel.

clue.text: Pierce got us a flat

definitions.meaning: to pierce is to make a hole in
what gave the car a deflated tyre

explanation.surface: Someone named Pierce found the couple an apartment.
explanation.definitionFit: To make a hole in something; also a hole in a tyre, which leaves it flat.

clue.text: Orient encounters reverse in this respect

parts.note: the Orient is the East, E

indicators.note: reverse tells us to read the word for encounters backwards

parts.note: meets means encounters

explanation.surface: The East meets a setback in some respect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reverse' turns MEETS into STEEM after E; 'in this' links.
explanation.definitionFit: High regard and admiration are the same as respect.
